newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil rallies as investment funds change tack.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil rallies as investment funds change tack.

text.p: A surprise rally on world oil markets, buoyed by investment fund buying, took crude higher again on Wednesday despite the burden of oversupply in the key Atlantic Basin crude market.
London futures for bellwether North Sea Brent blend rose nine cents on Wednesday morning to $20.34 a barrel on top of a Tuesday's 75-cent jump.
Dealers said the rise in the value of benchmark North Sea Brent blend was the result of a scramble by speculators to cover oversold positions on futures contracts in New York and London.
Investment fund managers moved swiftly to square their books ahead of the expiry of the April crude contract in New York on Thursday.
"What you saw was a very sharp short-covering rally," said Peter Gignoux, manager of the energy desk at brokers Smith Barney in London.

Clues to the surge in prices came in a report from the U.S. futures watchdog the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which showed three times more short sales than long purchases by speculators in the United States.

Also helping crude was the threat to Venezuelan oil exports from a controversial court ruling in the eastern town of Cabimas banning single-hull oil tankers from using the Maracaibo Lake shipping channel.
The ruling followed a 25,000 barrel oil spill in the area at the end of February. If ratified it would limit exports from the region to double-hulled tankers.

Venezuela, the single biggest supplier of oil to the U.S., would find difficulty maintaining exports while it scoured the world for double-hulled tankers, an official with state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said.
A barge accident on the Mississippi River, a vital link for petroleum product shipments into the Midwest United States, also underpinned oil prices.
The river remained closed indefinitely for a clean-up operation after a string of 25 barges hit a bridge in Baton Rouge, Louisiana late on Monday.
Technical analysts said oil had been overdue a recovery after the lengthy slide from near six-year highs at the beginning of the year and could move higher again before the end of the week.
Brent slipped to $18.68 a barrel two weeks ago from just below $25 in mid-January.

"This could be quite bullish, at least for the next one or two days," said Steve Kwan, a technical analyst at MMS International. "I expect we will create new short-term highs and push back above $20.50 towards $21."

But physical traders were taking a pessimistic view of the balance for supply and demand in the Atlantic Basin as North Sea spot market cargoes sold on Wednesday at large discounts versus the futures market.
"There's a wide divergence between what's happening on futures and what's happening on the physical market," said a trader.
"The only positive feature is that the contango (pricing physical oil at a discount) will encourage refiners to buy."
Dealers were looking for fresh signs of a rally in gasoline, which traditionally lends support to the oil complex in spring.

U.S. gasoline inventories are at a significant deficit to year-ago levels as the industry gears up for the spring and summer driving seasons. The American Petroleum Institute said late on Tuesday that gasoline supplies last week fell by 4.3 million barrels.
But uncertainties over the likely growth in U.S. gasoline demand this year so far has left many traders unsure how heavily they should bet on a gasoline rally.
